user_input: In DRF, when exactly do the authentication classes run relative to the rest of my view logic?
reference: Authentication is the very first thing a DRF view does. It runs before the permission and throttling checks and before any of your own view code.
reference_contexts: Authentication always runs at the very start of the view, before the permission and throttling checks occur, and before any other code is allowed to proceed.
llm_response: Authentication classes run at the very start of the view. They execute before permission and throttling checks occur, and before any other code is allowed to proceed.
llm_references:
Authentication - Django REST framework

Authentication

Auth needs to be pluggable.
— Jacob Kaplan-Moss,
"REST worst practices" (https://jacobian.org/writing/rest-worst-practices/)

Authentication is the mechanism of associating an incoming request with a set of identifying credentials, such as the user the request came from, or the token that it was signed with.  The
permission (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/)
and
throttling (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/throttling/)
policies can then use those credentials to determine if the request should be permitted.

REST framework provides several authentication schemes out of the box, and also allows you to implement custom schemes.

Authentication always runs at the very start of the view, before the permission and throttling checks occur, and before any other code is allowed to proceed.

The
`request.user`
property will typically be set to an instance of the
`contrib.auth`
package's
`User`
class.

The
`request.auth`
property is used for any additional authentication information, for example, it may be used to represent an authentication token that the request was signed with.

Note
Don't forget that
authentication by itself won't allow or disallow an incoming request
, it simply identifies the credentials that the request was made with.
For information on how to set up the permission policies for your API please see the
permissions documentation (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/)
.

user_input: Coming from plain Django I keep hunting for some kind of "login middleware" I can switch on so the whole API requires auth — but there doesn't seem to be one. What's the DRF way to set the authentication for every endpoint at once?
reference: Set them globally with DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES in your REST_FRAMEWORK settings dict; every view uses that default unless it overrides it per-view or per-viewset.
reference_contexts: The default authentication schemes may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES setting.

REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.authentication.BasicAuthentication' , 'rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication' , ] } You can also set the authentication scheme on a per-view or per-viewset basis, using the APIView class-based views.
llm_response:
To require authentication for every endpoint at once in Django REST framework, you should use the global settings in your `settings.py` file. 

While authentication classes identify the user, permission classes determine whether the request is granted or denied. To enforce that API requests are logged in, you must configure the following settings:

1.  **`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`**: Set this to define the authentication schemes (e.g., `BasicAuthentication` or `SessionAuthentication`).
2.  **`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`**: Set this to `['rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated']` to ensure that only authenticated users are granted access.

Example configuration in `settings.py`:

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.authentication.BasicAuthentication',
        'rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication',
    ],
    'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated',
    ]
}
```

This approach is the recommended mechanism for DRF views, as DRF views are opted-out of Django's `LoginRequiredMiddleware`. Using these global settings ensures that unauthenticated requests receive a 401 status code rather than being redirected to a login page.
llm_references:
The default authentication schemes may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
setting.  For example.

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.authentication.BasicAuthentication','rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication',]}`
```

You can also set the authentication scheme on a per-view or per-viewset basis,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.

```
`fromrest_framework.authenticationimportSessionAuthentication,BasicAuthenticationfromrest_framework.permissionsimportIsAuthenticatedfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassExampleView(APIView):authentication_classes=[SessionAuthentication,BasicAuthentication]permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'user':str(request.user),# `django.contrib.auth.User` instance.'auth':str(request.auth),# None}returnResponse(content)`
```

Or, if you're using the
`@api_view`
decorator with function based views.

```
`@api_view(['GET'])@authentication_classes([SessionAuthentication,BasicAuthentication])@permission_classes([IsAuthenticated])defexample_view(request,format=None):content={'user':str(request.user),# `django.contrib.auth.User` instance.'auth':str(request.auth),# None}returnResponse(content)`
```

The default permission policy may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
setting.  For example.

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated',]}`
```

If not specified, this setting defaults to allowing unrestricted access:

```
`'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.permissions.AllowAny',]`
```

You can also set the authentication policy on a per-view, or per-viewset basis,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.

```
`fromrest_framework.permissionsimportIsAuthenticatedfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassExampleView(APIView):permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'status':'request was permitted'}returnResponse(content)`
```

Or, if you're using the
`@api_view`
decorator with function based views.

```
`fromrest_framework.decoratorsimportapi_view,permission_classesfromrest_framework.permissionsimportIsAuthenticatedfromrest_framework.responseimportResponse@api_view(['GET'])@permission_classes([IsAuthenticated])defexample_view(request,format=None):content={'status':'request was permitted'}returnResponse(content)`
```

Note
When you set new permission classes via the class attribute or decorators you're telling the view to ignore the default list set in the
`settings.py`
file.

Provided they inherit from
`rest_framework.permissions.BasePermission`
, permissions can be composed using standard Python bitwise operators. For example,
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
could be written:

```
`fromrest_framework.permissionsimportBasePermission,IsAuthenticated,SAFE_METHODSfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassReadOnly(BasePermission):defhas_permission(self,request,view):returnrequest.methodinSAFE_METHODSclassExampleView(APIView):permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated|ReadOnly]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'status':'request was permitted'}returnResponse(content)`
```

Note
Composition of permissions supports the
`&`
(and),
`|`
(or) and
`~`
(not) operators, and also allows the use of brackets
`(`
`)`
to group expressions.
Operators follow the same precedence and associativity rules as standard logical operators (
`~`
highest, then
`&`
, then
`|`
).

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)
, please note that all views from DRF are opted-out of this middleware.  This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

Authentication or identification by itself is not usually sufficient to gain access to information or code.  For that, the entity requesting access must have authorization.
—
Apple Developer Documentation (https://developer.apple.com/library/mac/#documentation/security/Conceptual/AuthenticationAndAuthorizationGuide/Authorization/Authorization.html)

Together with
authentication (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/)
and
throttling (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/throttling/)
, permissions determine whether a request should be granted or denied access.

Permission checks are always run at the very start of the view, before any other code is allowed to proceed.  Permission checks will typically use the authentication information in the
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
properties to determine if the incoming request should be permitted.

Permissions are used to grant or deny access for different classes of users to different parts of the API.

The simplest style of permission would be to allow access to any authenticated user, and deny access to any unauthenticated user. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticated`
class in REST framework.

A slightly less strict style of permission would be to allow full access to authenticated users, but allow read-only access to unauthenticated users. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
class in REST framework.

user_input: What header and prefix does DRF's built-in TokenAuthentication expect for the token?
reference: Send it in the Authorization header prefixed with the literal word "Token" and a space, e.g. `Authorization: Token 9944...`. Subclass TokenAuthentication if you'd rather use a keyword like Bearer.
reference_contexts: key ) For clients to authenticate, the token key should be included in the Authorization HTTP header.

For example: Authorization : Token 9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b If you want to use a different keyword in the header, such as Bearer , simply subclass TokenAuthentication and set the keyword class variable.
llm_response: DRF's built-in `TokenAuthentication` expects the token to be included in the `Authorization` HTTP header. The token key must be prefixed by the string literal "Token", followed by whitespace.
llm_references:
Note
The token authentication provided by Django REST framework is a fairly simple implementation.
For an implementation which allows more than one token per user, has some tighter security implementation details, and supports token expiry, please see the
Django REST Knox (https://github.com/James1345/django-rest-knox)
third party package.

This authentication scheme uses a simple token-based HTTP Authentication scheme.  Token authentication is appropriate for client-server setups, such as native desktop and mobile clients.

To use the
`TokenAuthentication`
scheme you'll need to
configure the authentication classes (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/#setting-the-authentication-scheme)
to include
`TokenAuthentication`
, and additionally include
`rest_framework.authtoken`
in your
`INSTALLED_APPS`
setting:

```
`INSTALLED_APPS=[...'rest_framework.authtoken']`
```

Make sure to run
`manage.py migrate`
after changing your settings.

The
`rest_framework.authtoken`
app provides Django database migrations.

You'll also need to create tokens for your users.

```
`fromrest_framework.authtoken.modelsimportTokentoken=Token.objects.create(user=...)print(token.key)`
```

For clients to authenticate, the token key should be included in the
`Authorization`
HTTP header.  The key should be prefixed by the string literal "Token", with whitespace separating the two strings.  For example:

```
`Authorization:Token9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b`
```

If you want to use a different keyword in the header, such as
`Bearer`
, simply subclass
`TokenAuthentication`
and set the
`keyword`
class variable.

If successfully authenticated,
`TokenAuthentication`
provides the following credentials.

`request.user`
will be a Django
`User`
instance.
`request.auth`
will be a
`rest_framework.authtoken.models.Token`
instance.

Unauthenticated responses that are denied permission will result in an
`HTTP 401 Unauthorized`
response with an appropriate WWW-Authenticate header.  For example:

```
`WWW-Authenticate:Token`
```

The
`curl`
command line tool may be useful for testing token authenticated APIs.  For example:

```
`curl-X GET http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/example/ -H 'Authorization: Token 9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b'`
```

Note
If you use
`TokenAuthentication`
in production you must ensure that your API is only available over
`https`
.

user_input: What's the difference between IsAuthenticated and AllowAny?
reference: IsAuthenticated blocks anonymous users and lets logged-in users through; AllowAny lets every request through regardless of authentication.
reference_contexts: The IsAuthenticated permission class will deny permission to any unauthenticated user, and allow permission otherwise.
The AllowAny permission class will allow unrestricted access, regardless of if the request was authenticated or unauthenticated .
llm_response:
The difference between the two permission classes is as follows:

*   **`AllowAny`**: Allows unrestricted access to the API, regardless of whether the user is authenticated or unauthenticated [1].
*   **`IsAuthenticated`**: Denies access to any unauthenticated user and only allows access to registered (authenticated) users [2].
llm_references:
The
`AllowAny`
permission class will allow unrestricted access,
regardless of if the request was authenticated or unauthenticated
.

This permission is not strictly required, since you can achieve the same result by using an empty list or tuple for the permissions setting, but you may find it useful to specify this class because it makes the intention explicit.

The
`IsAuthenticated`
permission class will deny permission to any unauthenticated user, and allow permission otherwise.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to registered users.

user_input: How do I turn on pagination for my whole API, and what settings does it need?
reference: Set DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS and PAGE_SIZE globally in REST_FRAMEWORK. You need both — they're None by default.
reference_contexts: The pagination style may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS and PAGE_SIZE setting keys.

For example, to use the built-in limit/offset pagination, you would do something like this: REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS' : 'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination' , 'PAGE_SIZE' : 100 } Note that you need to set both the pagination class, and the page size that should be used.
llm_response:
To turn on pagination for your whole API, you must set the `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS` and `PAGE_SIZE` keys within the `REST_FRAMEWORK` setting in your configuration. Both are `None` by default.

### Required Settings
*   **`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`**: Specifies the pagination style to use. You can use built-in classes or a custom class.
*   **`PAGE_SIZE`**: Specifies the number of items per page.

### Available Built-in Styles
You can choose one of the following built-in classes for `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`:

1.  **`rest_framework.pagination.PageNumberPagination`**: Uses a page number in the query parameters (default parameter is `page`).
2.  **`rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination`**: Uses `limit` and `offset` query parameters. If `PAGE_SIZE` is set, the `limit` parameter becomes optional.
3.  **`rest_framework.pagination.CursorPagination`**: Uses an opaque cursor for pagination.

### Example Configuration
To enable a style globally, use the following format:

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS': 'rest_framework.pagination.PageNumberPagination',
    'PAGE_SIZE': 100
}
```

### Customizing Pagination
If you need to modify specific aspects (such as allowing clients to control page size or changing query parameter names), you should:
1.  Create a custom class by subclassing one of the built-in pagination classes and overriding its attributes (e.g., `page_size`, `page_query_param`, `page_size_query_param`, `max_page_size`).
2.  Set `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS` to the path of your custom class (e.g., `'my_project.apps.core.pagination.MyCustomPagination'`).
llm_references:
The pagination style may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
and
`PAGE_SIZE`
setting keys. For example, to use the built-in limit/offset pagination, you would do something like this:

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`
```

Note that you need to set both the pagination class, and the page size that should be used.  Both
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
and
`PAGE_SIZE`
are
`None`
by default.

You can also set the pagination class on an individual view by using the
`pagination_class`
attribute. Typically you'll want to use the same pagination style throughout your API, although you might want to vary individual aspects of the pagination, such as default or maximum page size, on a per-view basis.

To enable the
`PageNumberPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration, and set the
`PAGE_SIZE`
as desired:

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.PageNumberPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`
```

On
`GenericAPIView`
subclasses you may also set the
`pagination_class`
attribute to select
`PageNumberPagination`
on a per-view basis.

By default, the query parameter name used for pagination is
`page`
.
This can be customized by subclassing
`PageNumberPagination`
and overriding the
`page_query_param`
attribute.

For example:

```
`fromrest_framework.paginationimportPageNumberPaginationclassCustomPagination(PageNumberPagination):page_query_param='p'`
```

With this configuration, clients would request pages using
`?p=2`
instead of
`?page=2`
.

To enable the
`LimitOffsetPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration:

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination'}`
```

Optionally, you may also set a
`PAGE_SIZE`
key. If the
`PAGE_SIZE`
parameter is also used then the
`limit`
query parameter will be optional, and may be omitted by the client.

On
`GenericAPIView`
subclasses you may also set the
`pagination_class`
attribute to select
`LimitOffsetPagination`
on a per-view basis.

To enable the
`CursorPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration, modifying the
`PAGE_SIZE`
as desired:

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.CursorPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`
```

On
`GenericAPIView`
subclasses you may also set the
`pagination_class`
attribute to select
`CursorPagination`
on a per-view basis.

If you want to modify particular aspects of the pagination style, you'll want to override one of the pagination classes, and set the attributes that you want to change.

```
`classLargeResultsSetPagination(PageNumberPagination):page_size=1000page_size_query_param='page_size'max_page_size=10000classStandardResultsSetPagination(PageNumberPagination):page_size=100page_size_query_param='page_size'max_page_size=1000`
```

You can then apply your new style to a view using the
`pagination_class`
attribute:

```
`classBillingRecordsView(generics.ListAPIView):queryset=Billing.objects.all()serializer_class=BillingRecordsSerializerpagination_class=LargeResultsSetPagination`
```

Or apply the style globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
settings key. For example:

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'apps.core.pagination.StandardResultsSetPagination'}`
```

To have your custom pagination class be used by default, use the
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
setting:

```
`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'my_project.apps.core.pagination.LinkHeaderPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`
```

API responses for list endpoints will now include a
`Link`
header, instead of including the pagination links as part of the body of the response, for example:

A custom pagination style, using the 'Link' header

The
`PageNumberPagination`
class includes a number of attributes that may be overridden to modify the pagination style.

To set these attributes you should override the
`PageNumberPagination`
class, and then enable your custom pagination class as above.

`django_paginator_class`
- The Django Paginator class to use. Default is
`django.core.paginator.Paginator`
, which should be fine for most use cases.
`page_size`
- A numeric value indicating the page size. If set, this overrides the
`PAGE_SIZE`
setting. Defaults to the same value as the
`PAGE_SIZE`
settings key.
`page_query_param`
- A string value indicating the name of the query parameter to use for the pagination control.
`page_size_query_param`
- If set, this is a string value indicating the name of a query parameter that allows the client to set the page size on a per-request basis. Defaults to
`None`
, indicating that the client may not control the requested page size.
`max_page_size`
- If set, this is a numeric value indicating the maximum allowable requested page size. This attribute is only valid if
`page_size_query_param`
is also set.
`last_page_strings`
- A list or tuple of string values indicating values that may be used with the
`page_query_param`
to request the final page in the set. Defaults to
`('last',)`
. For example, use
`?page=last`
to go directly to the last page.
`template`
- The name of a template to use when rendering pagination controls in the browsable API. May be overridden to modify the rendering style, or set to
`None`
to disable HTML pagination controls completely. Defaults to
`"rest_framework/pagination/numbers.html"`
.

user_input: Once a list endpoint is paginated, what does the response body actually look like — how is a client supposed to know how many records exist in total and where to get the next batch?
reference: The results get wrapped in an envelope rather than returned as a bare array. A page-number paginated response carries `count` (the total number of records across all pages), `next` and `previous` (full URLs to the adjacent pages, or null at either end), and `results` (the records for this page). Clients walk the collection by following `next` until it comes back null, rather than by computing page numbers themselves.
reference_contexts: HTTP 200 OK { "count": 1023, "next": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=5", "previous": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=3", "results": [ ... ] }
llm_response:
When a list endpoint is paginated, the response body is a JSON object containing the following keys:

*   **`count`**: The total number of records available across all pages.
*   **`next`**: A URL string pointing to the next batch of records (or `null` if there is no next page).
*   **`previous`**: A URL string pointing to the previous batch of records (or `null` if there is no previous page).
*   **`results`**: An array containing the actual records for the current page.

The client determines the total number of records by reading the `count` field and retrieves the next batch by following the URL provided in the `next` field.
llm_references:
This pagination style mirrors the syntax used when looking up multiple database records. The client includes both a "limit" and an
"offset" query parameter. The limit indicates the maximum number of items to return, and is equivalent to the
`page_size`
in other styles. The offset indicates the starting position of the query in relation to the complete set of unpaginated items.

Request
:

```
`GET https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=400`
```

Response
:

```
`HTTP200OK{"count":1023,"next":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=500","previous":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=300","results":[…]}`
```

This pagination style accepts a single number page number in the request query parameters.

Request
:

```
`GET https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=4`
```

Response
:

```
`HTTP200OK{"count":1023,"next":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=5","previous":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=3","results":[…]}`
```

user_input: What do I set so clients can search my list endpoint with ?search=?
reference: Add DRF's SearchFilter to the view and give it a search_fields attribute; the filter only activates once search_fields is set.
reference_contexts: When in use, the browsable API will include a SearchFilter control: The SearchFilter class will only be applied if the view has a search_fields attribute set.
The search_fields attribute should be a list of names of text type fields on the model, such as CharField or TextField .
llm_response:
To enable searching on your list endpoint using `?search=`, you must perform the following steps:

1.  **Add `SearchFilter` to the view's `filter_backends`**: Include `filters.SearchFilter` in the `filter_backends` list of your view.
2.  **Set the `search_fields` attribute**: Define a `search_fields` attribute on your view, which should be a list of names of text type fields (e.g., `CharField` or `TextField`) on the model you wish to search.

Example implementation:

```python
from rest_framework import filters

class UserListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    serializer_class = UserSerializer
    filter_backends = [filters.SearchFilter]
    search_fields = ['username', 'email']
```

By default, the search parameter is named `'search'`. If you need to change this name, you can override it using the `SEARCH_PARAM` setting in your `REST_FRAMEWORK` configuration.
llm_references:
The
`SearchFilter`
class supports simple single query parameter based searching, and is based on the
Django admin's search functionality (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/contrib/admin/#django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin.search_fields)
.

When in use, the browsable API will include a
`SearchFilter`
control:

The
`SearchFilter`
class will only be applied if the view has a
`search_fields`
attribute set.  The
`search_fields`
attribute should be a list of names of text type fields on the model, such as
`CharField`
or
`TextField`
.


user_input: How do I let clients order list results but restrict which fields they can sort on?
reference: Use OrderingFilter and set an explicit ordering_fields list on the view so users can't sort on sensitive columns.
reference_contexts: It's recommended that you explicitly specify which fields the API should allow in the ordering filter.
You can do this by setting an ordering_fields attribute on the view, like so: class UserListView ( generics .
llm_response:
To allow clients to order list results while restricting the fields they can sort on, use the `OrderingFilter` class and explicitly define the allowed fields using the `ordering_fields` attribute on your view.

1.  Add `filters.OrderingFilter` to the `filter_backends` list in your view.
2.  Set the `ordering_fields` attribute to a list of the specific fields you want to permit.

Example:
```python
class UserListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    serializer_class = UserSerializer
    filter_backends = [filters.OrderingFilter]
    ordering_fields = ['username', 'email']
```

Clients can then order the results by adding the `ordering` query parameter to the URL (e.g., `?ordering=username` or `?ordering=-username` for reverse order). 

The documentation recommends this approach to prevent data leakage, such as exposing sensitive fields like password hashes. If you do not specify `ordering_fields`, the filter defaults to allowing ordering on any readable field on the serializer. Alternatively, if you are confident there is no sensitive data, you can set `ordering_fields = '__all__'` to allow ordering on any model field or queryset aggregate.

user_input: I've got a Spring background and I'm looking for DRF's equivalent of a DTO — something to turn a list of model objects into JSON in one shot. How do I serialize a whole queryset at once?
reference: Pass many=True when instantiating the serializer, then give it the queryset or list of objects.
reference_contexts: To serialize a queryset or list of objects instead of a single object instance, you should pass the many=True flag when instantiating the serializer.
llm_response:
To serialize a queryset or list of objects into JSON in one shot, you should pass the `many=True` flag when instantiating your serializer [1].

When you pass `many=True`, the framework automatically creates a `ListSerializer` instance to handle the collection [3]. You do not need to use `ListSerializer` directly; simply passing the `many=True` argument to your serializer class is the recommended approach [3].

Example usage:
```python
queryset = Book.objects.all()
serializer = BookSerializer(queryset, many=True)
serializer.data
```

Additionally, you can pass the following arguments when using `many=True` to control validation:
* `allow_empty`: Set to `False` to disallow empty lists (defaults to `True`).
* `max_length`: Set to a positive integer to limit the number of elements.
* `min_length`: Set to a positive integer to require a minimum number of elements.

`many=True`
flag when instantiating the serializer.  You can then pass a queryset or list of objects to be serialized.

```
`queryset=Book.objects.all()serializer=BookSerializer(queryset,many=True)serializer.data# [#     {'id': 0, 'title': 'The electric kool-aid acid test', 'author': 'Tom Wolfe'},#     {'id': 1, 'title': 'If this is a man', 'author': 'Primo Levi'},#     {'id': 2, 'title': 'The wind-up bird chronicle', 'author': 'Haruki Murakami'}# ]`
```

Serializers - Django REST framework

Serializers

Expanding the usefulness of the serializers is something that we would
like to address.  However, it's not a trivial problem, and it
will take some serious design work.
— Russell Keith-Magee,
Django users group (https://groups.google.com/d/topic/django-users/sVFaOfQi4wY/discussion)

Serializers allow complex data such as querysets and model instances to be converted to native Python datatypes that can then be easily rendered into
`JSON`
,
`XML`
or other content types.  Serializers also provide deserialization, allowing parsed data to be converted back into complex types, after first validating the incoming data.

The serializers in REST framework work very similarly to Django's
`Form`
and
`ModelForm`
classes. We provide a
`Serializer`
class which gives you a powerful, generic way to control the output of your responses, as well as a
`ModelSerializer`
class which provides a useful shortcut for creating serializers that deal with model instances and querysets.

The
`ListSerializer`
class provides the behavior for serializing and validating multiple objects at once. You won't
typically
need to use
`ListSerializer`
directly, but should instead simply pass
`many=True`
when instantiating a serializer.

When a serializer is instantiated and
`many=True`
is passed, a
`ListSerializer`
instance will be created. The serializer class then becomes a child of the parent
`ListSerializer`

The following argument can also be passed to a
`ListSerializer`
field or a serializer that is passed
`many=True`
:

`allow_empty`
: this is
`True`
by default, but can be set to
`False`
if you want to disallow empty lists as valid input.
`max_length`
: this is
`None`
by default, but can be set to a positive integer if you want to validate that the list contains no more than this number of elements.
`min_length`
: this is
`None`
by default, but can be set to a positive integer if you want to validate that the list contains no fewer than this number of elements.

user_input: Instead of marking every field read_only=True individually on my ModelSerializer, is there a shortcut?
reference: Yes — use the Meta option read_only_fields with a list/tuple of field names.
reference_contexts: You may wish to specify multiple fields as read-only.

ModelSerializer ): class Meta : model = Account fields = [ 'id' , 'account_name' , 'users' , 'created' ] read_only_fields = [ 'account_name' ] Model fields which have editable=False set, and AutoField fields will be set to read-only by default, and do not need to be added to the read_only_fields option.
llm_response:
Yes, you can use the `read_only_fields` Meta option. This option should be a list or tuple of field names.

It is declared as follows:

```python
class AccountSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Account
        fields = ['id', 'account_name', 'users', 'created']
        read_only_fields = ['account_name']
```

Additionally, `AutoField` fields and model fields with `editable=False` are set to read-only by default and do not need to be added to this option. 

Note that if a read-only field is part of a `unique_together` constraint, you must specify the field explicitly on the serializer with `read_only=True` and `default=…` instead of using `read_only_fields`.
llm_references:
You may wish to specify multiple fields as read-only. Instead of adding each field explicitly with the
`read_only=True`
attribute, you may use the shortcut Meta option,
`read_only_fields`
.

This option should be a list or tuple of field names, and is declared as follows:

```
`classAccountSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):classMeta:model=Accountfields=['id','account_name','users','created']read_only_fields=['account_name']`
```

Model fields which have
`editable=False`
set, and
`AutoField`
fields will be set to read-only by default, and do not need to be added to the
`read_only_fields`
option.

Note
There is a special-case where a read-only field is part of a
`unique_together`
constraint at the model level. In this case the field is required by the serializer class in order to validate the constraint, but should also not be editable by the user.
The right way to deal with this is to specify the field explicitly on the serializer, providing both the
`read_only=True`
and
`default=…`
keyword arguments.
One example of this is a read-only relation to the currently authenticated
`User`
which is
`unique_together`
with another identifier. In this case you would declare the user field like so:
```
`user=serializers.PrimaryKeyRelatedField(read_only=True,default=serializers.CurrentUserDefault())`
```
Please review the
Validators Documentation (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/validators/)
for details on the
UniqueTogetherValidator (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/validators/#uniquetogethervalidator)
and
CurrentUserDefault (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/validators/#currentuserdefault)
classes.

`raise_exception`

user_input: Where do I put validation for a single serializer field?
reference: Add a .validate_<field_name> method to your Serializer subclass — it works like Django forms' .clean_<field_name> and gets the field value.

This method takes the field value as its only argument and must return the validated value or raise a `serializers.ValidationError`. If the field is declared with `required=False` and is not included in the input, this validation step will not occur.

`Serializer`
subclass.  These are similar to the
`.clean_<field_name>`
methods on Django forms.

These methods take a single argument, which is the field value that requires validation.

Your
`validate_<field_name>`
methods should return the validated value or raise a
`serializers.ValidationError`
.  For example:

```
`fromrest_frameworkimportserializersclassBlogPostSerializer(serializers.Serializer):title=serializers.CharField(max_length=100)content=serializers.CharField()defvalidate_title(self,value):"""
Check that the blog post is about Django.
```

`<field_name>`

`required=False`
then this validation step will not take place if the field is not included.

user_input: What's a SerializerMethodField for?
reference: A read-only field whose value comes from a method on the serializer, letting you add arbitrary computed data to the output.
reference_contexts: This is a read-only field. It gets its value by calling a method on the serializer class it is attached to.

To use it:
1. Define the field in your serializer class.
2. Create a method on that same serializer class to return the desired data.
3. By default, the field looks for a method named `get_<field_name>`, but you can specify a different method name using the `method_name` argument.
4. The method must accept a single argument (the object being serialized) in addition to `self`.

user_input: How does the source argument on a serializer field work?
reference: source names the attribute used to populate the field; it can be a no-arg method or a dotted path like 'user.email' to traverse relations.
reference_contexts: The name of the attribute that will be used to populate the field.

The `source` argument specifies the attribute used to populate a serializer field. It functions in the following ways:

*   **Attribute Name:** By default, it uses the name of the field itself.
*   **Method:** It can be a method that takes only a `self` argument (e.g., `source='get_absolute_url'`).
*   **Dotted Notation:** It can traverse attributes using dotted notation (e.g., `source='user.email'`). When using this, you may need to provide a `default` value if an object is missing or empty during traversal. Additionally, you should use `prefetch_related` or `select_related` to avoid n+1 database problems.
*   **Entire Object:** Using `source='*'` passes the entire object to the field, which is useful for nested representations or when the field requires the complete object to determine its output.

user_input: In tests, how do I authenticate a request without the real credential flow?
reference: Use force_authenticate() to directly authenticate the request against a user (and optionally a token).
reference_contexts: To forcibly authenticate a request, use the force_authenticate() method.
llm_response:
To authenticate a request in tests without the real credential flow, you can use the `force_authenticate` method. The approach depends on the testing tool you are using:

### Using `APIClient`
If you are using `APIClient`, you can force all subsequent requests to be treated as authenticated by calling `.force_authenticate()` on the client instance:

```python
user = User.objects.get(username='lauren')
client = APIClient()
client.force_authenticate(user=user)
```

To unauthenticate subsequent requests, call the method again with `user=None`:
```python
client.force_authenticate(user=None)
```

### Using `APIRequestFactory`
If you are testing views directly using `APIRequestFactory`, you must use the `force_authenticate()` function on the request object itself:

```python
from rest_framework.test import force_authenticate

factory = APIRequestFactory()
user = User.objects.get(username='olivia')
request = factory.get('/accounts/django-superstars/')
force_authenticate(request, user=user)
```

You can also provide a token if required:
```python
force_authenticate(request, user=user, token=user.auth_token)
```

**Note:** When using `APIRequestFactory`, `force_authenticate` directly sets `request.user`. If you reuse the same user instance across tests that update the user state, you may need to call `refresh_from_db()` between tests.
llm_references:
Sometimes you may want to bypass authentication entirely and force all requests by the test client to be automatically treated as authenticated.

This can be a useful shortcut if you're testing the API but don't want to have to construct valid authentication credentials in order to make test requests.

```
`user=User.objects.get(username='lauren')client=APIClient()client.force_authenticate(user=user)`
```

To unauthenticate subsequent requests, call
`force_authenticate`
setting the user and/or token to
`None`
.

```
`client.force_authenticate(user=None)`
```

When testing views directly using a request factory, it's often convenient to be able to directly authenticate the request, rather than having to construct the correct authentication credentials.

To forcibly authenticate a request, use the
`force_authenticate()`
method.

```
`fromrest_framework.testimportforce_authenticate
factory=APIRequestFactory()user=User.objects.get(username='olivia')view=AccountDetail.as_view()# Make an authenticated request to the view...request=factory.get('/accounts/django-superstars/')force_authenticate(request,user=user)response=view(request)`
```

The signature for the method is
`force_authenticate(request, user=None, token=None)`
.  When making the call, either or both of the user and token may be set.

For example, when forcibly authenticating using a token, you might do something like the following:

```
`user=User.objects.get(username='olivia')request=factory.get('/accounts/django-superstars/')force_authenticate(request,user=user,token=user.auth_token)`
```

Note
`force_authenticate`
directly sets
`request.user`
to the in-memory
`user`
instance. If you are reusing the same
`user`
instance across multiple tests that update the saved
`user`
state, you may need to call
refresh_from_db() (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/models/instances/#django.db.models.Model.refresh_from_db)
between tests.

Note
When using
`APIRequestFactory`
, the object that is returned is Django's standard
`HttpRequest`
, and not REST framework's
`Request`
object, which is only generated once the view is called.
This means that setting attributes directly on the request object may not always have the effect you expect.  For example, setting
`.token`
directly will have no effect, and setting
`.user`
directly will only work if session authentication is being used.
```
`# Request will only authenticate if `SessionAuthentication` is in use.request=factory.get('/accounts/django-superstars/')request.user=user
response=view(request)`
```
If you want to test a request involving the REST framework’s 'Request' object, you’ll need to manually transform it first:
```
`classDummyView(APIView):...factory=APIRequestFactory()request=factory.get('/',{'demo':'test'})drf_request=DummyView().initialize_request(request)assertdrf_request.query_params=={'demo':['test']}request=factory.post('/',{'example':'test'})drf_request=DummyView().initialize_request(request)assertdrf_request.data.get('example')=='test'`
```

The
`login`
method functions exactly as it does with Django's regular
`Client`
class.  This allows you to authenticate requests against any views which include
`SessionAuthentication`
.

```
`# Make all requests in the context of a logged in session.client=APIClient()client.login(username='lauren',password='secret')`
```

To logout, call the
`logout`
method as usual.

```
`# Log outclient.logout()`
```

The
`login`
method is appropriate for testing APIs that use session authentication, for example web sites which include AJAX interaction with the API.

user_input: What's DRF's reverse() and how does it differ from Django's?
reference: rest_framework.reverse.reverse behaves like django.urls.reverse but returns a fully qualified URL using the request's host/port — so pass the request.
reference_contexts: Signature: reverse(viewname, *args, **kwargs) Has the same behavior as django.urls.reverse , except that it returns a fully qualified URL, using the request to determine the host and port.
llm_response:
DRF's `reverse()` is a function used to return fully qualified URLs. It has the same behavior as `django.urls.reverse`, with the exception that it uses the request to determine the host and port.

To use it, you should include the `request` as a keyword argument:

```python
from rest_framework.reverse import reverse

reverse('view-name', args=[arg], request=request)
```
llm_references: Returning URLs - Django REST framework

Signature:
`reverse(viewname, *args, **kwargs)`

Has the same behavior as
django.urls.reverse (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/urlresolvers/#reverse)
, except that it returns a fully qualified URL, using the request to determine the host and port.

You should
include the request as a keyword argument
to the function, for example:

```
`fromrest_framework.reverseimportreversefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewfromdjango.utils.timezoneimportnowclassAPIRootView(APIView):defget(self,request):year=now().year
data={...'year-summary-url':reverse('year-summary',args=[year],request=request)}returnResponse(data)`
```

user_input: What does @api_view do to a plain function view?
reference: It wraps the function so it gets a DRF Request and returns a DRF Response for the listed HTTP methods; by default only GET is accepted and others get a 405.
reference_contexts: By default only GET methods will be accepted. Other methods will respond with "405 Method Not Allowed".
llm_response:
The `@api_view` decorator performs the following actions on a plain function view:

*   **Request/Response Handling:** It ensures the view receives an instance of `Request` (instead of the standard Django `HttpRequest`) and allows the view to return a `Response` object (instead of a Django `HttpResponse`).
*   **Configuration:** It allows you to specify which HTTP methods the view should respond to via the `http_method_names` argument. By default, only `GET` methods are accepted; other methods will result in a `405 Method Not Allowed` response.
*   **Context and Processing:** It adds context to `Response` objects to enable content negotiation and ensures the view uses the default renderers, parsers, and authentication classes specified in the settings.
*   **Error Handling:** It handles `ParseError` exceptions that occur when accessing `request.data` with malformed input.
llm_references:
Signature:
`@api_view(http_method_names=['GET'])`

The core of this functionality is the
`api_view`
decorator, which takes a list of HTTP methods that your view should respond to. For example, this is how you would write a very simple view that just manually returns some data:

```
`fromrest_framework.decoratorsimportapi_viewfromrest_framework.responseimportResponse@api_view()defhello_world(request):returnResponse({"message":"Hello, world!"})`
```

This view will use the default renderers, parsers, authentication classes etc specified in the
settings (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/settings/)
.

By default only
`GET`
methods will be accepted. Other methods will respond with "405 Method Not Allowed". To alter this behavior, specify which methods the view allows, like so:

```
`@api_view(['GET','POST'])defhello_world(request):ifrequest.method=='POST':returnResponse({"message":"Got some data!","data":request.data})returnResponse({"message":"Hello, world!"})`
```

REST framework provides two wrappers you can use to write API views.

The
`@api_view`
decorator for working with function based views.
The
`APIView`
class for working with class-based views.

These wrappers provide a few bits of functionality such as making sure you receive
`Request`
instances in your view, and adding context to
`Response`
objects so that content negotiation can be performed.

The wrappers also provide behavior such as returning
`405 Method Not Allowed`
responses when appropriate, and handling any
`ParseError`
exceptions that occur when accessing
`request.data`
with malformed input.

Saying [that class-based views] is always the superior solution is a mistake.
—
Nick Coghlan (http://www.boredomandlaziness.org/2012/05/djangos-cbvs-are-not-mistake-but.html)

REST framework also allows you to work with regular function based views.  It provides a set of simple decorators that wrap your function based views to ensure they receive an instance of
`Request`
(rather than the usual Django
`HttpRequest`
) and allows them to return a
`Response`
(instead of a Django
`HttpResponse`
), and allow you to configure how the request is processed.

user_input: We're launching a mobile app with ~200k users and we don't want server-side sessions. I want each user to authenticate once and then send some credential on every request, and I need an endpoint that hands that credential back given a username and password. What's the DRF-native approach and what do I have to install/migrate?
reference: TokenAuthentication fits client-server setups like mobile apps. Enable it plus rest_framework.authtoken, run migrate, and expose the built-in obtain_auth_token view so clients POST username/password and get a token to send in the Authorization header.
reference_contexts: Token authentication is appropriate for client-server setups, such as native desktop and mobile clients.
REST framework provides a built-in view to provide this behavior.

The obtain_auth_token view will return a JSON response when valid username and password fields are POSTed to the view using form data or JSON: { 'token' : '9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b' } Note that the default obtain_auth_token view explicitly uses JSON requests and responses, rather than using default renderer and parser classes in your settings.
A list or tuple of authentication classes, that determines the default set of authenticators used when accessing the request.user or request.auth properties.
llm_response:
The DRF-native approach for your requirements is `TokenAuthentication`.

### Installation and Configuration
1.  **Add to `INSTALLED_APPS`**: Include `'rest_framework.authtoken'` in your `INSTALLED_APPS` setting.
2.  **Run Migrations**: Execute `python manage.py migrate` to create the necessary database tables for tokens.
3.  **Configure Authentication**: Set your authentication classes to include `TokenAuthentication`.

### Endpoint for Credentials
To provide an endpoint that returns a token given a username and password, add the built-in `obtain_auth_token` view to your `urls.py`:

```python
from rest_framework.authtoken import views
urlpatterns += [path('api-token-auth/', views.obtain_auth_token)]
```

This view accepts `username` and `password` via POST (JSON or form data) and returns a JSON response containing the token.

### Usage
*   **Client Requests**: Clients must include the token in the `Authorization` HTTP header, prefixed by the string "Token":
    `Authorization: Token 9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b`
*   **Security**: You must ensure your API is only available over `https` when using `TokenAuthentication` in production.

### Alternatives
If you require features such as token expiry, tighter security, or support for multiple tokens per user, the documentation recommends the third-party package **Django REST Knox**.

The

`https`

user_input: I want everyone to be able to browse my data, but only the user who created a record should be able to change or delete it. How do I structure this in DRF?
reference: Combine IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly with a custom object-level permission (IsOwnerOrReadOnly) whose has_object_permission allows safe methods for anyone and write methods only when obj.owner == request.user.
reference_contexts: BasePermission ): """ Custom permission to only allow owners of an object to edit it.
SAFE_METHODS : return True # Write permissions are only allowed to the owner of the snippet.
The IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly will allow authenticated users to perform any request.
llm_response:
To structure your API so that everyone can browse data but only the creator can modify or delete it, follow these steps:

### 1. Associate Users with Records
Ensure your model has an `owner` attribute. When creating a record, override the `.perform_create()` method in your view to associate the current user with the instance:

```python
def perform_create(self, serializer):
    serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)
```

### 2. Create a Custom Permission Class
Create a custom permission class that inherits from `permissions.BasePermission` and implements `has_object_permission`. This class allows read-only access (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) to everyone and restricts write access to the owner:

```python
from rest_framework import permissions

class IsOwnerOrReadOnly(permissions.BasePermission):
    """Custom permission to only allow owners of an object to edit it."""
    def has_object_permission(self, request, view, obj):
        # Read permissions are allowed to any request
        if request.method in permissions.SAFE_METHODS:
            return True
        # Write permissions are only allowed to the owner
        return obj.owner == request.user
```

### 3. Apply the Permission to the View
Add the custom permission to the `permission_classes` property of your view class. It is recommended to include `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly` alongside your custom permission:

```python
permission_classes = [permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly, IsOwnerOrReadOnly]
```

### Important Considerations
*   **Generic Views:** If you are using generic views, they will automatically call `check_object_permissions` for you. If you are writing custom views, you must manually call `self.check_object_permissions(request, obj)` after retrieving the object instance.
*   **List Views:** Generic views do not automatically apply object-level permissions to each instance in a list. If you need to restrict visibility in list views, you must filter the queryset separately.
*   **Creation:** Object-level permissions are not applied when creating objects because `get_object()` is not called. To restrict creation, implement the check in your serializer or override `perform_create` in your ViewSet.

Really we'd like all code snippets to be visible to anyone, but also make sure that only the user that created a code snippet is able to update or delete it.

To do that we're going to need to create a custom permission.

In the snippets app, create a new file,
`permissions.py`

```
`fromrest_frameworkimportpermissionsclassIsOwnerOrReadOnly(permissions.BasePermission):"""Custom permission to only allow owners of an object to edit it."""defhas_object_permission(self,request,view,obj):# Read permissions are allowed to any request,# so we'll always allow GET, HEAD or OPTIONS requests.ifrequest.methodinpermissions.SAFE_METHODS:returnTrue# Write permissions are only allowed to the owner of the snippet.returnobj.owner==request.user`
```

Now we can add that custom permission to our snippet instance endpoint, by editing the
`permission_classes`
property on the
`SnippetDetail`
view class:

```
`permission_classes=[permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly,IsOwnerOrReadOnly]`
```

Make sure to also import the
`IsOwnerOrReadOnly`
class.

```
`fromsnippets.permissionsimportIsOwnerOrReadOnly`
```

Now, if you open a browser again, you find that the 'DELETE' and 'PUT' actions only appear on a snippet instance endpoint if you're logged in as the same user that created the code snippet.

The following is an example of a permission class that checks the incoming request's IP address against a blocklist, and denies the request if the IP has been blocked.

```
`fromrest_frameworkimportpermissionsclassBlocklistPermission(permissions.BasePermission):"""
Global permission check for blocked IPs.
"""defhas_permission(self,request,view):ip_addr=request.META['REMOTE_ADDR']blocked=Blocklist.objects.filter(ip_addr=ip_addr).exists()returnnotblocked`
```

As well as global permissions, that are run against all incoming requests, you can also create object-level permissions, that are only run against operations that affect a particular object instance.  For example:

```
`classIsOwnerOrReadOnly(permissions.BasePermission):"""
Object-level permission to only allow owners of an object to edit it.
Assumes the model instance has an `owner` attribute.
"""defhas_object_permission(self,request,view,obj):# Read permissions are allowed to any request,# so we'll always allow GET, HEAD or OPTIONS requests.ifrequest.methodinpermissions.SAFE_METHODS:returnTrue# Instance must have an attribute named `owner`.returnobj.owner==request.user`
```

Note that the generic views will check the appropriate object level permissions, but if you're writing your own custom views, you'll need to make sure you check the object level permission checks yourself.  You can do so by calling
`self.check_object_permissions(request, obj)`
from the view once you have the object instance.  This call will raise an appropriate
`APIException`
if any object-level permission checks fail, and will otherwise simply return.

Also note that the generic views will only check the object-level permissions for views that retrieve a single model instance.  If you require object-level filtering of list views, you'll need to filter the queryset separately.  See the
filtering documentation (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/filtering/)
for more details.

Currently our API doesn't have any restrictions on who can edit or delete code snippets.  We'd like to have some more advanced behavior in order to make sure that:

Code snippets are always associated with a creator.
Only authenticated users may create snippets.
Only the creator of a snippet may update or delete it.
Unauthenticated requests should have full read-only access.

Right now, if we created a code snippet, there'd be no way of associating the user that created the snippet, with the snippet instance.  The user isn't sent as part of the serialized representation, but is instead a property of the incoming request.

The way we deal with that is by overriding a
`.perform_create()`
method on our snippet views, that allows us to modify how the instance save is managed, and handle any information that is implicit in the incoming request or requested URL.

On the
`SnippetList`
view class, add the following method:

```
`defperform_create(self,serializer):serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)`
```

The
`create()`
method of our serializer will now be passed an additional
`'owner'`
field, along with the validated data from the request.

For performance reasons the generic views will not automatically apply object level permissions to each instance in a queryset when returning a list of objects.

Often when you're using object level permissions you'll also want to
filter the queryset (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/filtering/)
appropriately, to ensure that users only have visibility onto instances that they are permitted to view.

Because the
`get_object()`
method is not called, object level permissions from the
`has_object_permission()`
method
are not applied
when creating objects. In order to restrict object creation you need to implement the permission check either in your Serializer class or override the
`perform_create()`
method of your ViewSet class.

To implement a custom permission, override
`BasePermission`
and implement either, or both, of the following methods:

`.has_permission(self, request, view)`
`.has_object_permission(self, request, view, obj)`

The methods should return
`True`
if the request should be granted access, and
`False`
otherwise.

If you need to test if a request is a read operation or a write operation, you should check the request method against the constant
`SAFE_METHODS`
, which is a tuple containing
`'GET'`
,
`'OPTIONS'`
and
`'HEAD'`
.  For example:

```
`ifrequest.methodinpermissions.SAFE_METHODS:# Check permissions for read-only requestelse:# Check permissions for write request`
```

Note
The instance-level
`has_object_permission`
method will only be called if the view-level
`has_permission`
checks have already passed. Also note that in order for the instance-level checks to run, the view code should explicitly call
`.check_object_permissions(request, obj)`
. If you are using the generic views then this will be handled for you by default. (Function-based views will need to check object permissions explicitly, raising
`PermissionDenied`
on failure.)

Custom permissions will raise a
`PermissionDenied`
exception if the test fails. To change the error message associated with the exception, implement a
`message`
attribute directly on your custom permission. Otherwise the
`default_detail`
attribute from
`PermissionDenied`
will be used. Similarly, to change the code identifier associated with the exception, implement a
`code`
attribute directly on your custom permission - otherwise the
`default_code`
attribute from
`PermissionDenied`
will be used.

```
`fromrest_frameworkimportpermissionsclassCustomerAccessPermission(permissions.BasePermission):message='Adding customers not allowed.'defhas_permission(self,request,view):...`
```

REST framework permissions also support object-level permissioning.  Object level permissions are used to determine if a user should be allowed to act on a particular object, which will typically be a model instance.

Object level permissions are run by REST framework's generic views when
`.get_object()`
is called.
As with view level permissions, an
`exceptions.PermissionDenied`
exception will be raised if the user is not allowed to act on the given object.

If you're writing your own views and want to enforce object level permissions,
or if you override the
`get_object`
method on a generic view, then you'll need to explicitly call the
`.check_object_permissions(request, obj)`
method on the view at the point at which you've retrieved the object.

This will either raise a
`PermissionDenied`
or
`NotAuthenticated`
exception, or simply return if the view has the appropriate permissions.

For example:

```
`defget_object(self):obj=get_object_or_404(self.get_queryset(),pk=self.kwargs["pk"])self.check_object_permissions(self.request,obj)returnobj`
```

Note
With the exception of
`DjangoObjectPermissions`
, the provided
permission classes in
`rest_framework.permissions`
do not
implement the
methods necessary to check object permissions.
If you wish to use the provided permission classes in order to check object
permissions,
you must
subclass them and implement the
`has_object_permission()`
method described in the
Custom
permissions (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/#custom-permissions)

user_input: When a user creates a record, I want its owner set automatically to whoever is logged in — the client should never send it. What's the clean way?

To set the owner automatically to the logged-in user without the client sending it, use `HiddenField` combined with `CurrentUserDefault`.

The clean way to implement this is:

1.  **Define the field in your serializer:** Use `serializers.HiddenField` with `default=serializers.CurrentUserDefault()`.

user_input: My API is getting hammered. I want to cap how many requests anonymous vs logged-in users can make per day. What's the mechanism and where do the numbers go?
reference: Enable AnonRateThrottle and UserRateThrottle as throttle classes and put the actual limits (like '100/day' and '1000/day') under DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES.
reference_contexts: The default throttling policy may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES and DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES settings.

REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle' , 'rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle' ], 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES' : { 'anon' : '100/day' , 'user' : '1000/day' } } The rates used in DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES can be specified over a period of second, minute, hour or day.
A list or tuple of throttle classes, that determines the default set of throttles checked at the start of a view.
llm_response:
To cap requests for anonymous and logged-in users, you should use the `AnonRateThrottle` and `UserRateThrottle` classes.

### Mechanism
You can set these globally by adding them to the `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES` setting in your `REST_FRAMEWORK` configuration:

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle',
        'rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle'
    ],
    'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES': {
        'anon': '100/day',
        'user': '1000/day'
    }
}
```

*   **`AnonRateThrottle`**: Restricts unauthenticated users based on their IP address.
*   **`UserRateThrottle`**: Restricts authenticated users based on their user ID. If a request is unauthenticated, it falls back to using the IP address.

### Where the numbers go
The specific request limits are defined in the `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES` dictionary within your `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings. 

*   The keys `'anon'` and `'user'` correspond to the default scopes for these throttle classes.
*   The values are strings specifying the rate (e.g., `'100/day'`). You can use `s`, `m`, `h`, or `d` to define the period.

### Alternative Approaches
*   **Per-view/viewset**: You can override the global policy by setting the `throttle_classes` attribute on an `APIView` or using the `@throttle_classes` decorator for function-based views.
*   **Custom Rates**: If you need multiple user throttle rates (e.g., burst vs. sustained), you can override `UserRateThrottle` to define a unique `scope` for each class and add those scopes to your `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`.

As with permissions, multiple throttles may be used.  Your API might have a restrictive throttle for unauthenticated requests, and a less restrictive throttle for authenticated requests.

Another scenario where you might want to use multiple throttles would be if you need to impose different constraints on different parts of the API, due to some services being particularly resource-intensive.

The application-level throttling that REST framework provides should not be considered a security measure or protection against brute forcing or denial-of-service attacks. Deliberately malicious actors will always be able to spoof IP origins. In addition to this, the built-in throttling implementations are implemented using Django's cache framework, and use non-atomic operations to determine the request rate, which may sometimes result in some fuzziness.

user_input: When the payment provider we call during checkout is slow or down, our endpoint currently returns a wall of HTML with a stack trace in it. I want it to answer with a clean, machine-readable 'try again shortly' that our clients can branch on, and I want to define that once rather than writing the same try/except into every view that touches the provider.
reference: Define your own exception type and raise it; the framework turns it into the response. Subclass APIException — the base class for exceptions raised inside an APIView or @api_view — and set `.status_code`, `.default_detail` and `.default_code` on the class, e.g. a ServiceUnavailable with status_code = 503 and a default_detail of 'Service temporarily unavailable, try again later.'. Then any view that raises it produces that response, handled centrally instead of per view, and the body comes back in the standard error shape with a `detail` key rather than as a Django HTML error page. Note the boundary: this handling only applies to responses generated by *raised* exceptions — a Response object you return directly from a view, such as an explicit HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST, never passes through it.
reference_contexts: The base class for all exceptions raised inside an APIView class or @api_view.
To provide a custom exception, subclass APIException and set the .status_code, .default_detail, and .default_code attributes on the class.
Subclasses of APIException raised inside REST framework.

Note that the exception handler will only be called for responses generated by raised exceptions. It will not be used for any responses returned directly by the view, such as the HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST responses that are returned by the generic views when serializer validation fails.
llm_response:
To handle exceptions globally and return a machine-readable response, you should implement a custom exception handler. This allows you to define the error response logic once rather than repeating it in every view.

### 1. Create a custom exception handler
Create a function that accepts the exception (`exc`) and the context (`context`). This function should return a `Response` object.

```python
from rest_framework.views import exception_handler
from rest_framework.response import Response
from rest_framework import status

def custom_exception_handler(exc, context):
    # Call REST framework's default exception handler first
    response = exception_handler(exc, context)

    # If the exception is one you want to catch (e.g., a specific provider error),
    # return a custom JSON response.
    if isinstance(exc, YourPaymentProviderException):
        return Response(
            {"detail": "try again shortly"}, 
            status=status.HTTP_503_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
        )

    return response
```

### 2. Configure the setting
Register your handler in your project's settings using the `EXCEPTION_HANDLER` key:

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'EXCEPTION_HANDLER': 'my_project.my_app.utils.custom_exception_handler'
}
```

### 3. Alternative for 500 errors
If you specifically want to ensure that all 500 errors return JSON instead of HTML, you can use the generic error view provided by Django REST framework. Set this in your URL configuration:

```python
handler500 = 'rest_framework.exceptions.server_error'
```

**Note:** The custom exception handler is only called for responses generated by raised exceptions; it will not be used for responses returned directly by a view (e.g., `HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST`).

user_input: Our mobile client only ever renders two columns from this endpoint but the payload carries about thirty, and on a slow connection that's the difference between a snappy list and a spinner. The web client needs the full object from the same endpoint. I'd rather not stand up a parallel serializer and a parallel URL just to serve a narrower version of the same record.
reference: You don't need a second serializer class — the field set is mutable at runtime. Once a serializer is initialized its fields are available as the `.fields` attribute, an ordinary dictionary you can read and modify, which lets you change what gets rendered (and the arguments on individual fields) per instance rather than at declaration time. The documented pattern is a DynamicFieldsModelSerializer: accept an extra `fields` keyword in __init__, pop it before calling super(), and then drop everything not requested from self.fields. Your view decides what to pass — typically driven by a query parameter — so UserSerializer(user) returns the full record and UserSerializer(user, fields=('id', 'email')) returns the narrow one from the same class and the same URL. If you'd rather not hand-roll it, drf-dynamic-fields provides a mixin that limits fields from a URL parameter, and drf-flex-fields additionally handles expanding primitive fields into nested ones.

Modifying the fields argument directly allows you to do interesting things such as changing the arguments on serializer fields at runtime, rather than at the point of declaring the serializer.

class DynamicFieldsModelSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer): """ A ModelSerializer that takes an additional `fields` argument that controls which fields should be displayed. """ def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): # Don't pass the 'fields' arg up to the superclass fields = kwargs.pop('fields', None) # Instantiate the superclass normally super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
print(UserSerializer(user)) {'id': 2, 'username': 'jonwatts', 'email': 'jon@example.com'} print(UserSerializer(user, fields=('id', 'email'))) {'id': 2, 'email': 'jon@example.com'}
The drf-dynamic-fields package provides a mixin to dynamically limit the fields per serializer to a subset specified by an URL parameter.

You can achieve this by creating a `DynamicFieldsModelSerializer` class that allows you to specify which fields to display at the point of initialization.

To implement this, define a serializer class that overrides the `__init__` method to accept a `fields` argument, which is then used to remove any fields from the serializer's `.fields` attribute that were not explicitly requested:

```python
class DynamicFieldsModelSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    """
    A ModelSerializer that takes an additional `fields` argument that
    controls which fields should be displayed.
    """
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        # Don't pass the 'fields' arg up to the superclass
        fields = kwargs.pop('fields', None)
        # Instantiate the superclass normally
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        if fields is not None:
            # Drop any fields that are not specified in the `fields` argument.
            allowed = set(fields)
            existing = set(self.fields)
            for field_name in existing - allowed:
                self.fields.pop(field_name)
```

By using this class, you can serve the full object by default and pass the `fields` argument when initializing the serializer for the mobile client to restrict the payload to only the two required columns.

user_input: I want a self-describing API I can click around in a browser during development, with JSON still the primary format. How do I set that up?
reference: Register JSONRenderer and BrowsableAPIRenderer under DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES. JSON stays primary while the browsable renderer shows an HTML page reusing the highest-priority renderer for the body.
reference_contexts: The default set of renderers may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES setting.

Renders data into HTML for the Browsable API: This renderer will determine which other renderer would have been given highest priority, and use that to display an API style response within the HTML page.

REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.renderers.JSONRenderer' , 'rest_framework.renderers.BrowsableAPIRenderer' , ] } You can also set the renderers used for an individual view, or viewset, using the APIView class-based views.

REST framework uses a simple style of content negotiation to determine which media type should be returned to a client, based on the available renderers, the priorities of each of those renderers, and the client's Accept: header.
llm_response:
To set up a self-describing API that allows you to click around in a browser while keeping JSON as the primary format, follow these steps:

### 1. Configure Global Renderers
Set `JSONRenderer` as the first item in your `DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES` setting. This ensures that JSON is the default format for clients that do not specify an `Accept` header, while still including the Browsable API for human-friendly interaction.

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.renderers.JSONRenderer',
        'rest_framework.renderers.BrowsableAPIRenderer',
    ]
}
```

### 2. Accessing Formats in the Browser
*   **Browsable API:** By default, when you navigate to the API in a browser, it will return the HTML browsable interface. This interface allows you to view resources and submit data via `POST`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` forms.
*   **JSON View:** To view the raw JSON response while in the browser, append `?format=json` to the URL.

### 3. Making URLs Clickable
To ensure your API is fully "clickable" for browsing, include fully-qualified URLs in your resource output. You should use the `reverse` helper provided by the `rest_framework` package to generate these URLs, which will then be automatically "urlized" in the Browsable API.

### 4. Individual View Configuration
If you prefer to set this on a per-view basis rather than globally, you can define the `renderer_classes` attribute on an `APIView` or use the `@renderer_classes` decorator on a function-based view, ensuring `JSONRenderer` and `BrowsableAPIRenderer` are included in the list.
